title: Two Sum
interviewQuestion: Given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.

story.setup: You're a cashier and a customer hands you a target bill amount. You need to find two coins from a pile that add up exactly to it, without checking every possible pair.
scenes: The naive cashier checks every coin against every other coin — two nested loops, O(n²), slow when the pile is huge.
A smarter cashier keeps a notebook: as each coin comes in, she writes down its value and where she put it.
Before writing a new coin down, she first asks the notebook: 'do I already have a coin worth (target - this coin)?' — a Dictionary lookup, O(1).
The moment the notebook says yes, she has her pair and stops immediately — one pass, no need to look twice.
story.moral: Trade a second loop for a hashmap lookup — remembering what you've seen is cheaper than re-scanning for it.

analogy: Two Sum is like a cashier who remembers every coin she's seen so far instead of re-checking the whole pile each time.
explanation:
Brute force checks every pair with nested loops, giving O(n²) time and O(1) space. The optimal approach uses a Dictionary<int,int> mapping value to index: for each element, compute the complement (target - current), and check if it's already in the dictionary before inserting the current element. If found, you've located both indices in a single pass.
This achieves O(n) time and O(n) space by trading memory for speed. The key insight is inserting AFTER checking, so you never match an element with itself, and the check-then-insert order naturally returns the earlier index first.
interviewAnswerShort: Use a Dictionary to store value-to-index as you iterate once; for each number check if target minus that number was already seen — O(n) time, O(n) space instead of brute force O(n²).
interviewAnswerDetailed: The brute-force solution compares every pair of numbers with two nested loops, which is O(n²) time and O(1) space — fine for small arrays but slow at scale. The optimized solution uses a single pass with a Dictionary<int,int> that maps each seen value to its index. For every number, I compute what I 'need' (target minus the current number) and check if that need already exists in the dictionary. If it does, I immediately return the stored index and the current index. If not, I add the current number and its index to the dictionary and move on. This turns the problem into O(n) time at the cost of O(n) extra space, which is almost always the right tradeoff since memory is cheaper than repeated computation. I'd also mention edge cases: no valid pair (return empty array), duplicate values (the dictionary correctly keeps the most recent index which still works since we check before inserting), and negative numbers (work fine since subtraction handles them naturally).

codeExample.explanation: A single forward pass with a Dictionary lookup turns Two Sum into O(n) time by checking for the needed complement before inserting the current value.

mistakes: Inserting the current number into the dictionary before checking for its complement, which can wrongly match a number with itself
Using nested loops (O(n²)) when a hashmap solves it in O(n)
Forgetting that the problem usually guarantees exactly one solution, so returning early is safe
Not handling duplicate values correctly (e.g., nums = [3,3], target = 6)

followUps.question: What if the array is sorted?
followUps.answer: Use two pointers from both ends: move left pointer up if sum is too small, right pointer down if too large — O(n) time, O(1) space, no extra memory needed.

followUps.question: What if you need ALL pairs, not just one?
followUps.answer: Iterate and store counts of each value; for each unique value check if its complement exists, being careful to avoid double-counting and to handle the case where a number pairs with itself.

followUps.question: Why not sort the array first?
followUps.answer: Sorting is O(n log n) and you'd lose the original indices unless you track them separately, so it's usually slower and more complex than the hashmap approach unless the array is already sorted.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Check before you insert — the receipt trick.
memoryHack.mnemonic: "Need it? Check the notebook. Not there? Write it down."
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture a cashier's notebook: each new coin first asks 'is my missing half already written here?' before adding itself to the page.

Use Dictionary<int,int> for O(1) average lookup instead of List.Contains which is O(n)
State the brute-force complexity first in interviews, then optimize — shows structured thinking
Handle the no-solution case explicitly (return empty array or throw, per requirements)

If the array is already sorted, two pointers gives O(n) time with O(1) space — better than the hashmap when sorting is free

title: Contains Duplicate / Find Duplicates in an Array
interviewQuestion: Given an array, determine if it contains any duplicate values, and separately, return the list of values that appear more than once.

story.setup: You're a bouncer at a VIP event with a guest list. Every guest who walks in gets checked against the list you've already recorded.
scenes: Each guest hands you their name; you try to ADD it to your VIP set.
HashSet.Add() itself tells you whether it succeeded — if it returns false, that name was already there.
The moment Add() fails, you've caught your duplicate on the spot, no need to scan the whole guest list again.
For 'who are ALL the repeat guests', you keep two sets: one for everyone seen, one for confirmed repeats.
story.moral: HashSet.Add returning a bool is a free duplicate detector — no need for a separate Contains check first.

analogy: Checking for duplicates is like a bouncer whose guest-list app tells him instantly if a name is already checked in.
explanation:
HashSet<T>.Add(item) returns false if the item already exists in the set, making it a natural one-line duplicate check without a separate Contains lookup. For a simple boolean answer, iterate once and return true the moment Add fails.
To collect ALL duplicated values, use two sets: one tracking everything seen, and one collecting items that fail to be added to the first (i.e., are duplicates). This is O(n) time and O(n) space. LINQ offers a more declarative one-liner: arr.GroupBy(x => x).Where(g => g.Count() > 1).Select(g => g.Key), though it's less efficient since GroupBy materializes all groups before filtering.
interviewAnswerShort: Use a HashSet and rely on Add() returning false when an item already exists — that single call both checks and inserts, giving O(n) time and O(n) space.
interviewAnswerDetailed: For a simple contains-duplicate check, I iterate through the array once and call HashSet.Add(n) for each element. Add returns false if the element was already present, so the moment it returns false I can immediately return true — meaning I don't need a separate ContainsKey check followed by an Add call, which would double the lookups. This is O(n) time and O(n) worst-case space. If the interviewer wants ALL duplicated values rather than a yes/no, I use two sets: a 'seen' set for everything encountered, and a 'duplicates' set that collects any value that fails to be added to 'seen'. I'd also mention the LINQ one-liner using GroupBy and filtering groups with Count() > 1, which reads cleanly but is less efficient since it must build and hold all groups in memory before filtering, versus the single-pass HashSet approach which can short-circuit.

codeExample.explanation: HashSet.Add's boolean return value doubles as a duplicate check, avoiding a separate Contains call.

mistakes: Calling Contains() then Add() separately, doing two lookups instead of one
Using a List instead of a HashSet, making Contains an O(n) scan each time (O(n²) overall)
Forgetting FindDuplicates needs a second set to avoid reporting the same duplicate multiple times
Using GroupBy for a simple boolean check when a HashSet short-circuits faster

followUps.question: How would you find duplicates using O(1) extra space?
followUps.answer: If values are guaranteed to be in range [1, n], you can negate the value at index |nums[i]|-1 as a marker; if you land on an already-negative value, that index+1 is a duplicate — sorts-in-place style trick.

followUps.question: What if the array is already sorted?
followUps.answer: Just compare each element to its neighbor in one pass — no extra space needed at all, O(n) time O(1) space.

followUps.question: Is HashSet.Add thread-safe?
followUps.answer: No — HashSet<T> is not thread-safe for concurrent writes; use ConcurrentDictionary or lock around it if accessed from multiple threads.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Add() IS the check — don't check twice.
memoryHack.mnemonic: "Add() lies only once — false means you've met before."
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture a bouncer's tablet where tapping 'Add Guest' itself flashes red if that guest is already inside — no separate lookup screen needed.

bestPractices: Use HashSet<T>.Add's return value instead of Contains+Add for a single O(1) operation
For duplicate collection, keep a separate 'seen' and 'duplicates' set to avoid double-reporting
Prefer the iterative HashSet approach over LINQ GroupBy when performance matters (single pass vs full materialization)
If value range is bounded, consider the in-place negation trick to save space

GroupBy allocates a group per unique key plus lists of members — heavier than a HashSet for a pure duplicate check
Sorting first gives O(n log n) time but O(1) extra space if you can't use a hash structure

title: Find Duplicate Characters in a Word (with Counts)
interviewQuestion: Given a word, find every character that repeats and how many times each one occurs.

story.setup: You're a librarian tallying how many times each letter tile appears in a Scrabble bag pulled from one word.
scenes: First pass: for every letter tile drawn, you tick a mark next to that letter on your tally sheet — a Dictionary<char,int>.
GetValueOrDefault(c) means you never have to check 'is this letter's row even on my sheet yet' — it just returns 0 for a new letter.
Second pass: you read your tally sheet and read out loud every letter with a count greater than one.
Two clean passes — one to count, one to report — beats trying to do both at once and getting confused.
story.moral: Separate 'counting' from 'reporting' into two clear passes — it's easier to reason about and just as fast, O(n).

analogy: Counting duplicate letters is like a librarian's two-pass tally: first count every tile, then read back only the ones you counted more than once.
explanation:
The approach uses a Dictionary<char,int> to count character frequencies in a first pass over the string, using GetValueOrDefault(c) to default missing keys to 0 without a separate existence check. A second pass over the dictionary entries prints every character whose count exceeds 1.
This is O(n) time (n = string length) and O(k) space where k is the number of distinct characters (bounded by alphabet size, so effectively O(1) for typical text). The LINQ equivalent — GroupBy(c => c).Where(g => g.Count() > 1) — expresses the same two-phase logic declaratively but at the cost of building full groups upfront.
interviewAnswerShort: Build a Dictionary<char,int> frequency map in one pass using GetValueOrDefault to accumulate counts, then iterate the dictionary and report any character with count greater than 1 — O(n) time, O(k) space.
interviewAnswerDetailed: I use a two-pass approach: pass one builds a Dictionary<char,int> where I increment each character's count using counts[c] = counts.GetValueOrDefault(c) + 1, which cleanly handles both new and existing characters without a manual ContainsKey check. Pass two iterates the dictionary entries and prints any character whose count is greater than 1. This runs in O(n) time where n is the string length, and O(k) space where k is the number of distinct characters — bounded and effectively constant for a fixed alphabet like ASCII or Unicode letters. I'd also mention the LINQ equivalent: input.GroupBy(c => c).Where(g => g.Count() > 1).Select(g => new { g.Key, Count = g.Count() }), which is more declarative but materializes all groups before filtering, so it's a bit heavier than the manual dictionary approach for very large inputs. If case-insensitivity matters, I'd normalize with ToLower() before counting.

codeExample.explanation: GetValueOrDefault avoids a manual ContainsKey check while accumulating character counts in a single pass, then a second pass filters for counts greater than one.

mistakes: Manually checking ContainsKey before incrementing instead of using GetValueOrDefault, which is more verbose and error-prone
Forgetting case sensitivity — 'A' and 'a' are different dictionary keys unless normalized
Trying to report duplicates in the same pass as counting, before you know the final count of a later-appearing character
Not handling non-letter characters (spaces, punctuation) if the requirement is letters only

followUps.question: How would you find the character with the HIGHEST count?
followUps.answer: Track a running max while building the dictionary, or after building it use counts.OrderByDescending(p => p.Value).First().

followUps.question: How would you make this case-insensitive?
followUps.answer: Normalize each character with char.ToLower(c) before using it as the dictionary key.

followUps.question: Can you do this without a dictionary, e.g., for lowercase-only ASCII?
followUps.answer: Yes — use an int[26] array indexed by c - 'a' as counts, which avoids hashing overhead and uses fixed O(1) space.

memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture a librarian's tally sheet: pass one taps a tick mark for every letter tile (defaulting new letters to zero), pass two reads back only the rows with more than one tick.

title: First Non-Repeated Character
interviewQuestion: Find the first character in a string that does not repeat.

story.setup: You're judging a talent show where every act performs once or twice. You need to announce, in the ORDER they first walked on stage, who was the first act to perform only once.
scenes: Round one: you tally how many times each act performed, without caring about order yet.
Round two: you walk through the program in the original order the acts appeared.
The moment you hit an act whose tally is exactly 1, that's your answer — first appearance order matters, not tally order.
A Dictionary alone can't preserve 'first in original order' — you need to re-walk the original sequence in round two.
story.moral: Counting doesn't remember order — you need a second pass over the ORIGINAL sequence to find the first unique one.

analogy: Finding the first non-repeated character is like re-reading the show program in order after tallying performances, to find the first act to perform exactly once.
explanation:
This requires two passes: the first builds a Dictionary<char,int> frequency count for every character (order doesn't matter here). The second pass re-iterates the ORIGINAL string in its original order, returning the first character whose count equals exactly 1.
The second pass is necessary because a dictionary doesn't preserve insertion or original order reliably for this purpose — you must walk the source string again to respect its original sequence. This is O(n) time and O(k) space, two linear passes rather than one, since the count of a character isn't final until the whole string has been scanned.
interviewAnswerShort: Count all characters into a Dictionary<char,int> in one pass, then re-scan the original string in order and return the first character whose count is exactly 1 — O(n) time, O(k) space.
interviewAnswerDetailed: I build a Dictionary<char,int> frequency map in a first pass over the string, incrementing each character's count. Then, critically, I do a SECOND pass — this time over the original string again, in its original order — and return the first character whose count in the dictionary equals 1. The second pass is required because the order characters were counted in a dictionary doesn't reliably reflect the string's original order for this purpose; you need to check candidates in the sequence they actually appeared. This is O(n) time overall (two linear passes) and O(k) space for the frequency map, where k is the number of distinct characters. A classic example is 'swiss', where 's' and 'i' each repeat, but 'w' is the first character with count 1, so the answer is 'w'. If no such character exists, I'd return a sentinel like '\0' or throw, depending on the contract.

codeExample.explanation: Two passes: count frequencies first, then re-walk the ORIGINAL string order to find the first character with a count of exactly 1.

mistakes: Trying to find the answer in a single pass, which is impossible since a character's total count isn't known until the string ends
Iterating the Dictionary in pass two instead of re-iterating the original string — dictionaries don't guarantee the original character order
Forgetting to handle the case where no character is unique (empty result)
Not accounting for case sensitivity if the problem expects case-insensitive comparison

followUps.answer: Same two-pass approach, but iterate the original string backwards in pass two, or track the last index of each count-1 character.

followUps.question: Can you solve this in one pass?
followUps.answer: Not with a simple count-and-check, but you can use an ordered structure like a LinkedHashMap-equivalent (Dictionary + a separate insertion-order list) to track candidates as you go and remove them when they repeat — still effectively O(n) but more complex.

title: Reverse a String (with a Loop)
interviewQuestion: Reverse a string without using a built-in Reverse method, and also handle reversing the words in a sentence.

story.setup: Picture two people standing at opposite ends of a line of chairs, each holding a name tag. They swap tags and both step one chair inward, again and again, until they meet in the middle.
scenes: Because C# strings are immutable, you first copy the string into a char array — you need mutable chairs to swap tags on.
Left pointer starts at index 0, right pointer starts at the last index.
Each step: swap the characters at left and right, then move left forward and right backward.
When left meets or passes right, everyone has swapped — the array is reversed in place, O(n) time, O(1) extra space beyond the array copy.
story.moral: Two pointers walking toward each other from both ends is the go-to pattern for in-place reversal.

analogy: Reversing a string is like two people at opposite ends of a row of chairs swapping name tags and stepping inward until they meet.
explanation:
Since C# strings are immutable, you must first convert to a char[] with ToCharArray() to mutate in place. Two pointers start at opposite ends (l=0, r=length-1); each iteration swaps arr[l] and arr[r], then increments l and decrements r, stopping when l >= r.
This is O(n) time and O(n) space (for the char array copy, since the original string can't be mutated). A common follow-up is reversing WORDS in a sentence rather than characters: split on spaces, reverse the array of words with Array.Reverse, and rejoin with string.Join — a different granularity of the same two-pointer/reversal idea.
interviewAnswerShort: Convert the string to a char array (since strings are immutable), then use two pointers from both ends swapping characters and moving inward until they meet — O(n) time, O(n) space.
interviewAnswerDetailed: Strings in C# are immutable, so the first step is always ToCharArray() to get a mutable copy. Then I use the classic two-pointer technique: left starts at index 0, right starts at the last index. In a while loop that continues while left is less than right, I swap arr[left] and arr[right] using tuple deconstruction, then increment left and decrement right. When they meet or cross, the array is fully reversed, and I construct a new string from it. This is O(n) time and O(n) space, since we can't avoid the copy given string immutability. A very common follow-up is reversing the WORDS in a sentence rather than the characters — for that, I split the string on spaces (using StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries to handle multiple spaces), call Array.Reverse on the resulting word array, and rejoin with string.Join(' ', words). So 'the sky is blue' becomes 'blue is sky the'. Same underlying idea — reversal — but applied at word granularity instead of character granularity.

title: Palindrome — String and Number
interviewQuestion: Determine whether a string is a palindrome, and separately, whether an integer is a palindrome without converting it to a string.

story.setup: You're checking if a word looks the same in a mirror. For a NUMBER version, you're not allowed to write it on paper (convert to string) — you must fold it in your head using only arithmetic.
scenes: For a string, two people stand at opposite ends and compare letters, walking inward — if any pair mismatches, it's not a mirror image.
For a number, you peel off the last digit with x % 10 and build a 'reversed' number digit by digit, like rebuilding the mirror image from the tail.
You stop HALFWAY — once your rebuilt reversed number is >= the shrinking original, you've covered half the digits, no need to fully reverse (which risks overflow anyway).
Compare the two halves: for even-length numbers they should be equal; for odd-length, drop the reversed number's last digit (the middle one) before comparing.
story.moral: You don't need to fully reverse a number to check symmetry — reversing HALF avoids overflow and does half the work.

analogy: Checking a numeric palindrome is like folding a number in half using arithmetic instead of writing it out and reading it backward.
explanation:
For a string palindrome, use two pointers from both ends comparing characters, moving inward, returning false on any mismatch — O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
For a number palindrome without converting to a string, negative numbers are never palindromes, and numbers ending in 0 (except 0 itself) can't be palindromes either (since a palindrome can't start with 0). The trick is to reverse only HALF the digits: repeatedly do rev = rev*10 + x%10 and x /= 10 until x <= rev, meaning you've processed at least half the digits. Then compare: for even digit counts, x == rev; for odd digit counts, the middle digit is in rev's last position, so compare x == rev/10. This avoids overflow risk from fully reversing a large number (e.g., reversing int.MaxValue would overflow) and is O(d) time, O(1) space where d is the digit count.
interviewAnswerShort: For strings, use two pointers comparing from both ends. For numbers, reverse only HALF the digits using arithmetic (no string conversion) to avoid overflow, then compare the two halves.
interviewAnswerDetailed: For a string palindrome check, I use two pointers — left at 0, right at length-1 — comparing characters and moving inward, returning false immediately on any mismatch. That's O(n) time, O(1) extra space. For the numeric version — often asked as a harder follow-up specifically to avoid converting to a string — I first rule out negative numbers (never palindromes due to the minus sign) and numbers ending in 0 unless the number itself is 0 (since a palindrome can't have a leading zero after reversal). Then I reverse only HALF the digits: in a loop, I do rev = rev * 10 + x % 10 and x /= 10, continuing while x > rev. Once x <= rev, I've processed at least half the digits. For an even number of digits, the two halves should be exactly equal (x == rev); for an odd number of digits, the middle digit ends up as the last digit of rev, so I compare x == rev / 10 to drop it before comparing. This is deliberately more clever than fully reversing the number: reversing all the digits of a large int risks integer overflow, and stopping at the halfway point avoids that risk entirely while doing half the work.

title: Prime Number Check
interviewQuestion: Write a function to check whether a given number is prime, and explain why you only loop up to its square root.

story.setup: You're a detective checking if a number has any 'partners' (factors) other than 1 and itself. You realize you don't need to interrogate every suspect up to n — only up to √n.
scenes: You start checking factors from 2 upward: does 2 divide n? Does 3? Does 4?
Then you notice: factors always come in PAIRS that multiply to n — like 2 and 50 for n=100.
If one factor of a pair is bigger than √n, its partner MUST be smaller than √n — you'd have already caught it.
So checking past √n is pointless — you've already met every possible 'partner' by then. Stop at i*i <= n.
story.moral: Factors pair up around the square root — checking beyond √n is redundant work that finds nothing new.

analogy: Checking primality is like verifying a number's factor pairs — you only need to check up to its square root because factor partners mirror around it.
explanation:
A number n is prime if it has no divisors other than 1 and itself. The naive check loops from 2 to n-1, which is O(n). The key optimization: factors come in pairs (a, b) where a*b = n; if a > √n, then b must be < √n, meaning any factor pair has at least one member <= √n. So you only need to check divisors up to and including √n.
The implementation checks n <= 1 (not prime), n == 2 (prime, the only even prime), then even numbers > 2 (not prime), then loops i from 3 to i*i <= n, incrementing by 2 (skipping even numbers since they're already ruled out). This reduces time complexity from O(n) to O(√n), which is what interviewers are specifically testing when they ask 'why i*i <= n'.
interviewAnswerShort: Loop divisors only up to √n instead of n, because if n has a factor larger than √n, it must also have a paired factor smaller than √n — so you'd have already found it. This cuts time from O(n) to O(√n).
interviewAnswerDetailed: To check if n is prime, I first handle edge cases: numbers <= 1 are not prime, 2 is prime (the only even prime), and any other even number is not prime. Then I loop odd divisors i starting from 3, checking if n % i == 0, but only while i*i <= n — this is the key optimization interviewers want to hear explained. The reasoning is that factors of n always come in pairs (a, b) such that a * b = n. If a is greater than √n, then b must be less than √n (otherwise a*b would exceed n). So if n has ANY factor greater than √n, it necessarily has a paired factor smaller than √n, which my loop would have already caught. This means checking divisors beyond √n is provably redundant — there's nothing left to find. This optimization brings time complexity from O(n) down to O(√n), and I increment by 2 instead of 1 since even divisors are already ruled out by the earlier even check, halving the remaining work again.

Not handling n <= 1 explicitly (0, 1, and negative numbers are not prime by definition)

followUps.question: Why increment i by 2 instead of 1 in the loop?
followUps.answer: Because the n % 2 == 0 check already ruled out all even divisors, so only odd numbers 3, 5, 7... can possibly be factors, halving the remaining iterations.

followUps.question: Is i*i <= n safe from overflow for large int n?
followUps.answer: For int n up to int.MaxValue (~2.1 billion), i can be up to ~46341, and i*i could overflow if using int for i without care near the boundary; using long for the i*i computation, or i <= n / i, avoids that risk.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
interviewQuestion: Given an array of stock prices by day, find the maximum profit from a single buy and a single sell (buy must occur before sell).

story.setup: You're a trader watching a stock's price tick by every day. You can only buy once and sell once — and you must buy BEFORE you sell.
scenes: You walk through the days one at a time, always remembering the LOWEST price you've seen SO FAR — your best possible buy point up to now.
At each new day, you ask: 'if I sell today, having bought at my lowest-so-far, what's my profit?'
If that hypothetical profit beats your best profit recorded so far, you update your record.
You never need to look backward or try every pair — the lowest price so far is always your best available buy, updated as you walk forward.
story.moral: Track the running minimum as you go — you never need to revisit the past to know your best buy point.

analogy: Buy-sell-stock is like a trader who only remembers the lowest price seen so far and checks daily if selling now beats their record profit.
explanation:
The naive approach checks every buy-sell pair, giving O(n²) time. The optimal greedy approach makes a single pass, tracking two running values: minPrice (the lowest price seen so far) and maxProfit (the best profit found so far).
For each price, first update minPrice if the current price is lower; otherwise, check if selling today (current price - minPrice) beats maxProfit and update if so. Because minPrice always reflects a day BEFORE the current one (or the current day itself, which yields 0 profit — never negative), the buy-before-sell constraint is automatically satisfied. This is O(n) time and O(1) space.
interviewAnswerShort: Track the minimum price seen so far in a single pass; at each day, compute profit as current price minus that minimum, and keep the maximum such profit — O(n) time, O(1) space.
interviewAnswerDetailed: The brute force tries every pair of buy day and later sell day, which is O(n²). The optimal solution is a single-pass greedy algorithm using two variables: minPrice, initialized to int.MaxValue, and maxProfit, initialized to 0. As I iterate through the prices array, for each price I check: if it's lower than minPrice, update minPrice — this day becomes the new best possible buy point. Otherwise, I compute the hypothetical profit if I sold today having bought at minPrice, and if that profit exceeds maxProfit, I update maxProfit. Because minPrice is always a price from a day at or before the current day, this naturally enforces buy-before-sell without extra bookkeeping. If prices only decrease across the whole array, maxProfit correctly stays 0 since no positive profit is ever possible. This is O(n) time and O(1) space — a single pass, constant extra memory.

codeExample.explanation: A single pass tracks the running minimum price and the best profit achievable by selling at each subsequent day.

mistakes: Using nested loops to check every buy/sell pair — O(n²) when O(n) is achievable
Forgetting to initialize minPrice to int.MaxValue (or the first price), causing incorrect comparisons on day one
Allowing a 'sell before buy' scenario by not correctly tracking that minPrice always represents an earlier or equal day
Confusing this with the 'multiple transactions allowed' variant, which uses a different (sum of all positive deltas) approach

followUps.question: What if you're allowed multiple buy/sell transactions (Stock II)?
followUps.answer: Sum every positive day-over-day price increase: profit += Math.Max(0, prices[i] - prices[i-1]) for each day — this captures all upward movements without needing to track specific buy/sell points.

followUps.question: What if there's a transaction fee per trade (Stock with Transaction Fee)?
followUps.answer: Use dynamic programming with two states per day: 'holding stock' and 'not holding stock', updating each based on the previous day's states minus the fee when selling.

followUps.question: What if you're limited to at most 2 transactions (Stock III)?
followUps.answer: Track four variables: buy1, sell1, buy2, sell2, representing the best profit achievable after each stage, updated greedily in a single pass — a classic DP-with-constant-state pattern.

memoryHack.mnemonic: "minPrice never looks back, maxProfit never forgets."
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture a trader with a sticky note that only ever gets updated to a LOWER buy price, while a separate note tracks the biggest profit spotted so far — both updated in a single walk down the price chart.

title: Plus One (Big Number as Digit Array)
interviewQuestion: Given a non-negative integer represented as an array of its digits, add one to it and return the new array of digits.

story.setup: You're an old-fashioned accountant adding 1 to a number so large it's written across a whole ledger row, one digit per cell — too big to fit in any calculator.
scenes: You start at the RIGHTMOST cell, the ones place, and add 1.
If the digit is less than 9, you simply increment it and you're done instantly — no other cell changes.
If it's a 9, it rolls over to 0 and you carry the +1 to the cell on its LEFT, repeating the same check.
If the carry rolls all the way past the leftmost cell (all 9s, like 999), you need a brand NEW cell at the front — the array grows by one, becoming 1000.
story.moral: Simulate carry propagation from the right, just like manual addition on paper — and be ready to grow the array by one digit for the all-9s edge case.

analogy: Plus One on a digit array is like an accountant adding 1 to a number too large for any calculator, carrying by hand from the rightmost column.
explanation:
The digits array represents a number too large for standard numeric types (a 100-digit number would overflow int, long, and even decimal), so the addition must be simulated digit by digit from the rightmost (least significant) position.
Iterate from the last index backward: if the current digit is less than 9, increment it and return immediately — no further carry needed. If it's 9, set it to 0 (the carry rolls over) and continue to the next digit leftward. If the loop completes without an early return, every digit was 9 (e.g., 999), meaning the result needs one more digit than the input — allocate a new array of length+1, set its first element to 1 (the rest default to 0), and return that. This is O(n) time and O(1) extra space in the common case, O(n) space only in the all-9s edge case.

interviewAnswerDetailed: The digits array represents a number that could be arbitrarily large — far beyond what int, long, or even decimal can hold, which is exactly why it's represented as an array in the first place rather than converted to a numeric type. I simulate manual addition: starting from the last index (the ones place) and moving left, if digits[i] is less than 9, I simply increment it and return the array immediately, since no carry is needed further left. If digits[i] equals 9, incrementing it would roll over to 10, so I set it to 0 and let the loop continue to carry into the next digit to the left. If the loop finishes without returning — meaning every digit was a 9, like [9,9,9] — the result must grow by one digit: I allocate a new int array of length digits.Length + 1, leave it zero-initialized except for setting index 0 to 1, giving [1,0,0,0] for the [9,9,9] input, correctly representing 1000. This is O(n) time; space is O(1) in the common case and O(n) only for the all-9s edge case where a new array must be allocated.

title: Roman to Integer
interviewQuestion: Convert a Roman numeral string (e.g., "MCMXCIV") to its integer value.

story.setup: You're reading an ancient Roman inscription, symbol by symbol, adding up values — but the Romans had a clever trick: putting a smaller symbol BEFORE a bigger one means SUBTRACT, not add.
scenes: Normally, you just add each symbol's value as you read left to right: V + I + I = VII = 7.
But sometimes a smaller symbol sits just before a bigger one, like IV — that's their shorthand for 'one less than five', i.e., 4, not 5+1=6.
So before adding a symbol's value, you peek at the NEXT symbol: if it's bigger, you SUBTRACT the current one instead of adding it.
"MCMXCIV" reads as M(1000) + CM(900, since C<M) + XC(90, since X<C) + IV(4, since I<V) = 1994.
story.moral: One lookahead comparison — smaller before bigger means subtract — decodes the entire subtractive notation trick.

analogy: Roman numeral parsing is like reading an inscription where a smaller symbol placed just before a bigger one flips it into a subtraction.
explanation:
Map each Roman character to its value using a Dictionary<char,int>. Iterate through the string left to right; for each character, compare its value to the NEXT character's value (if one exists). If the current value is less than the next value (e.g., 'I' before 'V'), subtract the current value from the total (handling the subtractive pairs IV, IX, XL, XC, CD, CM); otherwise, add it.
This single-pass lookahead approach correctly decodes both additive notation (VII = 5+1+1=7) and subtractive notation (IV = 5-1=4) without needing special-case string matching for each of the six subtractive pairs. It's O(n) time and O(1) space (the dictionary has a fixed 7 entries).
interviewAnswerShort: Map each symbol to its value in a Dictionary, then iterate left to right comparing each symbol's value to the next: if current is less than next, subtract it; otherwise add it — O(n) time, O(1) space.
interviewAnswerDetailed: I use a Dictionary<char,int> mapping each Roman numeral character (I, V, X, L, C, D, M) to its value. Then I iterate through the string from left to right with an index i, and for each character I look ahead to the next character (if i+1 is within bounds). If the current character's value is LESS than the next character's value — like I before V in 'IV' — that indicates subtractive notation, so I subtract the current value from the running total instead of adding it. Otherwise, I add it normally. This single lookahead comparison elegantly handles all six subtractive pairs (IV=4, IX=9, XL=40, XC=90, CD=400, CM=900) without needing to special-case-match each pair as a substring. Walking through 'MCMXCIV': M(1000, added since next is C which is smaller) + C(subtracted since next M is bigger, contributing -100) + M(added, +1000, giving CM=900 total) + X(subtracted since next C is bigger) + C(added, giving XC=90) + I(subtracted since next V is bigger) + V(added, giving IV=4) = 1000+900+90+4 = 1994. This is O(n) time and O(1) space.

Forgetting the bounds check (i + 1 < s.Length) before looking at the next character, causing an IndexOutOfRangeException on the last character
Not validating input for malformed Roman numerals (e.g., 'IIII' or 'VV') if the problem requires strict validation
Using a switch statement per character instead of a Dictionary, making the code more verbose without benefit

title: Linked List — The Five Classics
interviewQuestion: Solve the five most-asked linked list problems: reverse a list, detect a cycle, find the middle node, merge two sorted lists, and remove the Nth node from the end.

story.setup: Picture a treasure hunt with a chain of clue cards, each pointing to the next. Five classic challenges test how well you can manipulate that chain.
scenes: REVERSE: you walk the chain holding three cards at once — previous, current, next — flipping each arrow to point backward before stepping forward.
CYCLE DETECTION: a tortoise and a hare walk the chain at different speeds; if the chain loops back on itself, the hare eventually LAPS the tortoise and they meet again.
MIDDLE NODE: same tortoise-and-hare trick — when the hare reaches the end, the tortoise (moving half as fast) is standing exactly at the middle.
MERGE TWO SORTED LISTS: two chains, each already sorted, get zipped together by always picking the smaller front card, using a dummy 'placeholder' card to simplify the start.
REMOVE NTH FROM END: send a scout N steps ahead first, then walk scout and a trailing pointer together — when scout falls off the end, the trailing pointer sits right before the node to remove.
story.moral: Most linked list problems reduce to holding the right number of pointers (2 or 3) and moving them at the right relative speeds.

analogy: Linked list problems are a treasure-hunt chain of cards — reversal flips arrows with three hands, cycle/middle detection uses a tortoise and hare, merging zips two sorted chains, and removing the Nth-from-end uses a scout pointer running ahead.
explanation:
Reverse: iteratively walk the list holding prev, cur, and next pointers; at each step save next, redirect cur.next to prev, then advance prev and cur — O(n) time, O(1) space.
Cycle detection (Floyd's algorithm): a slow pointer moves 1 step, a fast pointer moves 2 steps per iteration; if there's a cycle, fast eventually catches up to slow inside the loop (they can't both circle forever without meeting since fast gains one position on slow each iteration); if fast reaches null, there's no cycle. O(n) time, O(1) space.
Middle node: the same slow/fast pointer trick — when fast reaches the end (or one before it), slow is at the middle, since slow moves at half the speed.
Merge two sorted lists: use a dummy head node to avoid special-casing the first insertion, then repeatedly attach the smaller of the two current nodes to the tail, advancing that list's pointer; at the end, attach whichever list has leftover nodes.
Remove Nth from end: advance a fast pointer n steps ahead first, then move both fast and a trailing pointer together until fast reaches the end; the trailing pointer is now positioned just before the node to remove, allowing an O(n) single-pass solution without knowing the list's length upfront.
interviewAnswerShort: Reverse uses prev/cur/next pointer rotation; cycle detection and finding the middle both use Floyd's slow/fast pointers; merging sorted lists uses a dummy head and picks the smaller front node each time; removing the Nth-from-end sends a pointer N steps ahead first, then moves both together.
interviewAnswerDetailed: These five problems cover the core linked-list toolkit. Reversing a list iteratively holds three pointers — prev (starts null), cur (starts at head), and a temporary next — at each step you save cur.next before overwriting it to point backward at prev, then shift prev and cur forward by one; at the end, prev is the new head. This is O(n) time, O(1) space. Cycle detection uses Floyd's Tortoise and Hare: a slow pointer advances one node per step, a fast pointer advances two; if there's a cycle, fast will eventually lap slow and they'll meet at the same node inside the loop; if fast (or fast.next) hits null first, there's no cycle — also O(n)/O(1). Finding the middle node reuses the exact same slow/fast mechanism: since fast moves twice as fast as slow, by the time fast reaches the end, slow has covered exactly half the distance and sits at the middle. Merging two sorted lists uses a dummy sentinel head node so the loop logic doesn't need a special case for the very first node — I compare the current nodes of both lists, attach the smaller one to the tail, and advance that list's pointer; once one list is exhausted, I attach the remainder of the other list directly (since it's already sorted). Removing the Nth node from the end is a classic single-pass trick: advance a 'fast' pointer n steps ahead of a 'slow' pointer first, then move both together one step at a time; when fast reaches the end, slow is positioned exactly at the node before the one to remove, letting you unlink it in one pass without first counting the list's total length.

followUps.question: How would you reverse a linked list recursively?
followUps.answer: Base case: if head is null or head.next is null, return head. Otherwise, recursively reverse the rest, then set head.next.next = head and head.next = null, returning the new head from the recursive call — O(n) time but O(n) stack space, versus O(1) space iteratively.

title: Array Classics
interviewQuestion: Solve five classic in-place array problems: move zeroes to the end, find the maximum subarray sum, rotate an array by k, find the second largest element, and merge two sorted arrays in place.

story.setup: Picture organizing a bookshelf where books (numbers) need reshuffling — some in place, some pushed to the end, some rotated, all without buying a second shelf (O(1) space).
scenes: MOVE ZEROES: a librarian slides every non-empty book to the front of the shelf, then fills the remaining slots at the end with blanks (zeroes) — one 'insert' pointer tracks where the next real book goes.
KADANE'S MAX SUBARRAY: walking the shelf, at each book you decide 'do I extend my current winning streak, or start fresh from here?' — keep whichever running streak is currently best.
ROTATE BY K: instead of shifting one book at a time k times, you cleverly reverse the WHOLE shelf, then reverse each of the two resulting sections — three reversals net a rotation.
SECOND LARGEST: one pass down the shelf, tracking both your current champion and runner-up, updating both as you go — no need to sort first.

MERGE TWO SORTED SHELVES IN PLACE: when one shelf has extra empty slots at the end, you fill it from the BACK — placing the largest remaining book from either shelf into the last open slot, working backward to avoid overwriting unmerged data.
story.moral: Most array tricks are either two-pointer in-place rearrangement, one-pass running-state tracking, or filling from the correct direction to avoid overwriting data you still need.

analogy: Array classics are like reorganizing a bookshelf in place — sliding real books forward, tracking win-streaks, reversing sections to rotate, and filling merged space from the back to avoid overwriting.
explanation:
Move Zeroes: use an 'insert' pointer starting at 0; for each non-zero element, place it at nums[insert] and increment insert; after the pass, fill all remaining positions from insert to the end with 0. This preserves relative order of non-zero elements in O(n) time, O(1) space.
Kadane's Max Subarray: track 'current' (the best sum ending at the current position) and 'best' (the best sum seen overall). At each element, current = Math.Max(nums[i], current + nums[i]) — either extend the existing subarray or start fresh at the current element — then update best = Math.Max(best, current). O(n) time, O(1) space.
Rotate Right by K: use the triple-reversal trick — reverse the entire array, then reverse the first k elements, then reverse the remaining n-k elements. This achieves an in-place rotation in O(n) time, O(1) space, avoiding a naive O(n*k) shift-by-one-k-times approach.
Second Largest: single pass tracking two variables, first and second (largest and second largest seen so far), updating both appropriately as each new element is compared — O(n) time, O(1) space, no sorting required.
Merge Two Sorted Arrays In Place: when one array has trailing empty space to accommodate the merge, fill from the BACK (largest indices first), comparing the largest remaining elements of each array and placing the bigger one at the current back position — this avoids overwriting elements in the first array that haven't been compared yet, which filling from the front would cause.
interviewAnswerShort: Move Zeroes uses an insert pointer for non-zero elements then pads zeroes; Kadane's tracks a running current/best sum; rotation uses triple reversal; second largest tracks two running maxes in one pass; merging sorted arrays in place fills from the back to avoid overwrites.
interviewAnswerDetailed: These five array patterns cover the most common in-place manipulation questions. Move Zeroes uses a single 'insert' pointer: as I scan the array, every non-zero element gets written to nums[insert] and insert increments; after the scan, everything from insert onward gets set to 0 — this preserves the relative order of non-zero elements in O(n)/O(1). Kadane's algorithm for max subarray sum tracks two running values: 'current', the best sum ending exactly at the current index, computed as Math.Max(nums[i], current + nums[i]) — meaning at each element I decide whether extending the previous subarray is still beneficial or whether starting fresh here is better — and 'best', the maximum current value seen so far; also O(n)/O(1). Rotating an array right by k uses a clever triple-reversal: reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k elements, then reverse the remaining elements — this achieves the rotation in O(n) time and O(1) space without the O(n*k) cost of naive one-step-at-a-time rotation. Finding the second largest element in one pass tracks two variables — first (largest so far) and second (second largest so far) — updating both correctly as each element is compared, avoiding a full sort which would cost O(n log n) versus this O(n) approach. Merging two sorted arrays in place — where the first array has trailing empty capacity to hold both — is a classic 'fill from the back' problem: you compare the largest remaining unmerged elements from each array and place the bigger one into the current back-most open slot, working backward; this specifically avoids the front-to-back approach's flaw of overwriting elements in the first array that haven't been compared and placed yet.

title: Dictionary/HashSet Classics
interviewQuestion: Solve five classic hashmap/hashset problems: valid anagram, group anagrams, word frequency count, majority element, and array intersection.

story.setup: You're running a word-sorting office where letters and words are filed, tallied, and voted on using nothing but Dictionaries and HashSets.
scenes: VALID ANAGRAM: count every letter of word 1 UP and every letter of word 2 DOWN in the same tally sheet — if you end at all zeroes, they're anagrams.
GROUP ANAGRAMS: file each word into a folder labeled by its letters SORTED alphabetically — 'eat', 'tea', 'ate' all land in the folder labeled 'aet'.
WORD FREQUENCY: split a sentence into words and let GroupBy count how many times each word shows up — one LINQ line does it.
MAJORITY ELEMENT: run an election where every vote for your current 'candidate' adds a point and every vote against subtracts one; if you ever hit zero, elect a new candidate — Boyer-Moore voting.
INTERSECTION: two guest lists compared with a HashSet lookup or LINQ's Intersect finds who's on BOTH lists in O(n+m).
story.moral: Dictionary and HashSet turn counting, grouping, voting, and comparing problems into single linear passes.

analogy: Hashmap classics are like a word-sorting office: tallying letters for anagram checks, filing by sorted-letter folders for grouping, counting votes for the majority element, and comparing guest lists for intersections.
explanation:
Valid Anagram: use one Dictionary<char,int>, incrementing counts for every character in string s and decrementing for every character in string t; if all counts end at zero (and lengths match), they're anagrams. O(n) time, O(k) space.
Group Anagrams: for each word, compute a canonical key by sorting its characters alphabetically (e.g., 'eat'->'aet'); use that key in a Dictionary<string,List<string>> to group all words sharing the same sorted-letter signature. O(n*k log k) time (k = avg word length for the sort), O(n*k) space.
Word Frequency: text.Split(' ').GroupBy(w => w).ToDictionary(g => g.Key, g => g.Count()) is a one-line LINQ solution counting occurrences of each word.
Majority Element (Boyer-Moore voting): track a candidate and a vote counter; if votes hits 0, the current element becomes the new candidate; increment votes if the current element matches the candidate, decrement otherwise. The element appearing more than n/2 times will always survive as the final candidate. O(n) time, O(1) space — no hashmap needed at all.
Intersection: use HashSet.Contains lookups, or LINQ's a.Intersect(b), to find common elements between two collections in O(n+m) time.
interviewAnswerShort: Valid Anagram counts characters up for one string and down for the other, checking all zeroes; Group Anagrams keys by sorted characters; Word Frequency uses GroupBy; Majority Element uses Boyer-Moore voting (O(1) space, no hashmap); Intersection uses HashSet lookups.
interviewAnswerDetailed: Valid Anagram checks if two strings are letter-for-letter rearrangements of each other. I use a single Dictionary<char,int>: increment the count for each character in the first string, decrement for each character in the second string; if every count ends at exactly zero (and the lengths matched initially), they're anagrams — O(n) time, O(k) space where k is alphabet size. Group Anagrams takes a list of words and buckets them by which words are anagrams of each other; the trick is computing a canonical signature for each word by sorting its characters alphabetically — 'eat', 'tea', and 'ate' all produce the signature 'aet' — then using a Dictionary<string,List<string>> keyed by that signature to collect the groups; O(n*k log k) time due to the per-word sort. Word Frequency is a classic LINQ one-liner: text.Split(' ').GroupBy(w => w).ToDictionary(g => g.Key, g => g.Count()) counts occurrences of each word in a sentence. Majority Element — finding the element appearing more than n/2 times — has an elegant O(1)-space solution called Boyer-Moore voting: maintain a 'candidate' and a 'votes' counter starting at 0; for each element, if votes is 0, that element becomes the new candidate; then increment votes if the element matches the candidate, else decrement. Mathematically, the true majority element (appearing more than half the time) always survives this process as the final candidate, since it can 'outvote' every other element combined. Finally, Intersection of two arrays or collections is solved with a HashSet for O(1) average lookups, or the LINQ a.Intersect(b) one-liner, both achieving O(n+m) time.

codeExample.explanation: Five hashmap/hashset patterns: counting-up-and-down for anagrams, sorted-key grouping, LINQ GroupBy counting, Boyer-Moore voting for O(1)-space majority detection, and Intersect/HashSet for set overlap.

followUps.answer: Because a true majority element (appearing more than n/2 times) can 'cancel out' every other element paired against it and still have votes remaining at the end — mathematically it's guaranteed to survive as the final candidate.

followUps.question: What if there's no guaranteed majority element — how do you verify the candidate?
followUps.answer: Do a second pass counting actual occurrences of the candidate and check if that count exceeds n/2; if not, no majority element exists.

followUps.question: How would you find all elements appearing MORE than n/3 times (Majority Element II)?
followUps.answer: Extend Boyer-Moore voting to track two candidates and two vote counters simultaneously, since at most two elements can appear more than n/3 times, then verify both with a second counting pass.

title: Infinite Loops and FizzBuzz
interviewQuestion: Show the different ways to write an infinite loop in C#, identify a common accidental infinite loop bug, and implement FizzBuzz.

story.setup: You're a warehouse worker on a conveyor belt that never stops — sometimes on purpose (an intentional infinite loop waiting for external events), sometimes by accident (a forgotten increment leaves you stuck forever).
scenes: INTENTIONAL: a server's main loop is written as while(true) on purpose — it should run forever until an external signal (like Ctrl+C or a cancellation token) stops it.
ACCIDENTAL: a junior dev writes while (i < 5) { Console.WriteLine(i); } and forgets i++ — the belt never advances, the same item printed forever, CPU pegged at 100%.

FizzBuzz tests whether you can juggle THREE conditions cleanly: divisible by 15 (both 3 and 5) must be checked FIRST, before the individual 3-only or 5-only checks, or you'd never reach the combined case.
A nested ternary expresses all four branches (FizzBuzz, Fizz, Buzz, number) in one readable line, checking the most SPECIFIC condition (divisible by 15) first.
story.moral: Infinite loops are a tool when intentional and a bug when accidental — the difference is always whether the exit condition can actually be reached.

analogy: An infinite loop is a conveyor belt that runs forever on purpose (waiting for a stop signal) or by accident (a forgotten increment) — FizzBuzz tests ordering your conditions from most to least specific.
explanation:
C# offers three equivalent ways to write an intentional infinite loop: while(true){}, for(;;){}, and do{}while(true);. These are legitimate for scenarios like server listen loops, game loops, or polling loops, typically broken out of with a break statement or an external cancellation signal.
An ACCIDENTAL infinite loop, a common interview 'spot the bug' question, happens when a loop's exit condition can never become false — classically, forgetting to increment the loop variable (e.g., while(i<5){...} with no i++ inside), leaving i permanently unchanged and the condition permanently true.
FizzBuzz (1 to 100): print 'FizzBuzz' if divisible by 15, 'Fizz' if only by 3, 'Buzz' if only by 5, else the number itself. The ORDER of checks matters — checking divisibility by 15 first (or checking 3 and 5 together) is required, because checking 3 or 5 individually first would never let you reach the combined case, since any number divisible by 15 is also divisible by 3 and 5 individually.
interviewAnswerShort: Infinite loops (while(true), for(;;), do-while(true)) are intentional when waiting for an external stop signal, but accidental when a loop's exit condition can never change (e.g., a forgotten increment). FizzBuzz requires checking the combined divisible-by-15 case before the individual 3-only/5-only checks.
interviewAnswerDetailed: C# has three syntactically different but functionally identical ways to write an infinite loop: while(true){}, for(;;){} (all three for-clauses omitted), and do{}while(true);. These are intentional and legitimate in scenarios like a server's request-handling loop, a game's render loop, or a polling loop — they're meant to run until an external condition (a cancellation token, a break statement, a received signal) stops them. The interview 'gotcha' variant is spotting an ACCIDENTAL infinite loop: a classic example is while (i < 5) { Console.WriteLine(i); } where the developer forgot to include i++ inside the loop body — since i never changes, the condition i < 5 remains true forever, and the loop prints 0 endlessly while consuming 100% of a CPU core. For FizzBuzz, the standard implementation loops from 1 to 100 and for each number checks: is it divisible by 15 (both 3 and 5)? Print 'FizzBuzz'. Else, divisible by 3 only? Print 'Fizz'. Else, divisible by 5 only? Print 'Buzz'. Else, print the number itself. The critical detail interviewers watch for is checking the combined divisible-by-15 condition FIRST (or checking both 3 and 5 as a compound condition before the individual checks) — because any number divisible by 15 is ALSO divisible by 3 and by 5 individually, so if you check %3==0 first, you'd incorrectly print just 'Fizz' for 15 and never reach the 'FizzBuzz' branch.

codeExample.explanation: Intentional infinite loops rely on an external break/return; an accidental one is missing a variable update; FizzBuzz's nested ternary checks the most specific (divisible by 15) condition first.

mistakes: Checking n % 3 == 0 before n % 15 == 0 in FizzBuzz, causing multiples of 15 to incorrectly print only 'Fizz'
Forgetting to increment/update the loop control variable, causing an unintentional infinite loop that pegs the CPU
Using while(true) without any break or external cancellation mechanism in production code, leaving no way to stop it gracefully
Using string concatenation instead of a switch expression or ternary chain for FizzBuzz, making the code harder to read

followUps.question: How would you write FizzBuzz using a switch expression instead of nested ternaries?
followUps.answer: switch ((n % 3, n % 5)) { case (0, 0) => "FizzBuzz", case (0, _) => "Fizz", case (_, 0) => "Buzz", _ => n.ToString() } — a C# 8+ tuple pattern switch expression, arguably more readable than nested ternaries.

followUps.question: How do you gracefully stop an intentional while(true) loop in a real application?
followUps.answer: Use a CancellationToken checked each iteration (while (!token.IsCancellationRequested)), or a break statement triggered by an internal condition, or in async contexts, await a signal like a SemaphoreSlim or channel.

followUps.question: What tools would you use to detect an accidental infinite loop in production?
followUps.answer: CPU usage monitoring/alerting (a pegged core), application performance monitoring (APM) tools showing a request that never completes, or attaching a debugger to inspect the stuck thread's call stack and variable state.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Check the most SPECIFIC condition first — 15 before 3 or 5.
memoryHack.mnemonic: "FizzBuzz: 15 first, or Fizz steals Buzz's thunder."
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture a conveyor belt inspector who checks the RAREST label first (both Fizz AND Buzz stickers) before checking for just one sticker — checking the common label first would mean the rare double-labeled item never gets its correct tag.

bestPractices: Always check the most specific (combined) condition before the individual conditions in FizzBuzz-style branching
Ensure every intentional infinite loop has a reachable break condition or external cancellation mechanism
Double-check loop variables are actually updated inside the loop body during code review — a classic silent bug
Prefer a switch expression with tuple patterns over deeply nested ternaries for readability in modern C#
performanceTips: An accidental infinite loop pegs a CPU core at 100% and can starve other threads/requests — always verify loop termination conditions
FizzBuzz itself is O(n) with O(1) per-iteration work — trivial performance-wise, the focus is on correctness and code clarity
Use CancellationToken-based loops in async code instead of raw while(true) for cooperative, responsive cancellation

options: Any number divisible by 15 is also divisible by 3 and 5, so checking those individually first would prevent ever reaching the combined 'FizzBuzz' case
C# requires conditions in numeric order
quiz.explanation: Since multiples of 15 satisfy both n%3==0 and n%5==0, checking either individual condition first would incorrectly short-circuit before the combined case is checked.

quiz.question: What is the bug in: int i = 0; while (i < 5) { Console.WriteLine(i); }?
options: i is never incremented inside the loop, causing an infinite loop
quiz.explanation: Without i++ inside the loop body, i remains 0 forever, so the condition i < 5 never becomes false.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT a valid way to write an intentional infinite loop in C#?
quiz.explanation: C# has no `loop` keyword; while(true), for(;;), and do-while(true) are the three standard forms.

flashcards.back: while(true){}, for(;;){}, do{}while(true);
Forgetting to update the loop control variable (e.g., missing i++).
Check divisible-by-15 (or combined 3-and-5) FIRST, before individual 3-only or 5-only checks.

flashcards.front: Graceful way to stop an intentional infinite loop?
flashcards.back: Check a CancellationToken or break condition each iteration.

title: Complexity Revision Table
interviewQuestion: Summarize the time and space complexity of the classic coding problems, and describe your live-coding protocol for tackling a new problem in an interview.

story.setup: You're a coach reviewing game film with the team before the big match — a cheat sheet of every play (algorithm) and how fast/efficient it was, plus the pre-match routine every player follows.
scenes: The coach's whiteboard lists every play: Two Sum uses the 'remember what you've seen' trick, Kadane uses the 'extend or restart' trick, cycle detection uses the 'fast catches slow' trick.
Almost every play on the board falls into just TWO families: two pointers (converging or racing) or a hash lookup (remembering what's been seen) — the meta-pattern.

Before every match, players run the same six-step warmup: state the naive play, propose the upgrade, run the play while narrating, walk through one example, state the final speed/memory cost, and call out the risky edge cases.
That warmup routine — not raw talent — is what separates a player who freezes under pressure from one who methodically works through any new problem thrown at them.
story.moral: Almost every classic algorithm is a two-pointer trick or a hash lookup — and a structured live-coding routine turns unfamiliar problems into familiar patterns.

analogy: The complexity table is a coach's cheat sheet of every play and its speed, and the live-coding protocol is the pre-match warmup every player runs before tackling a new opponent.
explanation:
The recurring meta-pattern across nearly all classic coding interview problems is one of two techniques: TWO POINTERS (converging from both ends like palindrome/reverse-string, or racing at different speeds like Floyd's cycle detection, or a lead-then-follow gap like remove-Nth-from-end) or a HASH LOOKUP (remembering seen values in O(1), like Two Sum, duplicates, and anagram grouping).

interviewAnswerDetailed: Looking across the classic coding problems, almost everything reduces to one of two meta-patterns: two pointers or a hash lookup. Two pointers shows up as converging pointers from both ends (palindrome check, string reversal), racing pointers at different speeds (Floyd's cycle detection, finding the middle of a linked list), or a lead-then-follow gap (removing the Nth node from the end, or the sliding window family). Hash lookups show up whenever you need O(1) 'have I seen this before' checks — Two Sum, duplicate detection, anagram grouping, word frequency. Beyond recognizing the pattern, I have the complexity table memorized as a sanity check: Two Sum and duplicate detection are O(n) time/O(n) space; buy-sell-stock, plus-one, cycle detection, reverse-linked-list, Kadane's max subarray, array rotation, and majority element are all O(n) time but only O(1) space since they avoid extra hash structures; prime checking is the outlier at O(√n) time due to the square-root optimization. For any NEW problem I haven't seen before, I follow a consistent six-step live-coding protocol: first, I state the brute-force solution and its complexity out loud, even if I know it's not optimal — this shows I understand the baseline. Second, I propose the optimization and explain WHY it helps (usually 'trade space for time' via a hash structure, or 'avoid redundant work' via two pointers). Third, I write the code while narrating my reasoning step by step. Fourth, I dry-run the code against one concrete example to catch bugs before claiming it's done. Fifth, I explicitly state the final time and space complexity. Sixth, I proactively call out edge cases: empty input, a single-element input, all-negative values, potential integer overflow, and null references — showing defensive, production-minded thinking rather than just solving the happy path.

followUps.question: How do you handle a problem where you genuinely don't recognize the pattern?
